title: Does digital transformation of high-carbon emission enterprises promote green technological innovation quality? —The moderating role of executive green awareness and corporate social responsibility
summary: High-carbon industries face immense pressure to achieve substantive green innovation. While digital transformation (DT) is a potential catalyst, its impact on the quality of green technological innovation (GTI) remains unclear. Using panel data from 291 Chinese A-share listed firms in high-carbon sectors, this study employs fixed-effects models to investigate whether DT promotes GTI quality. We further examine the moderating roles of executive green awareness (EGA) and corporate social responsibility (CSR), and the boundary condition of the emission trading scheme (ETS) policy. The fixed-effects models reveal that: (1) DT significantly improves GTI quality, with persistent effects. (2) EGA and CSR positively moderate this relationship, strengthening the link between DT and high-quality GTI. (3) Heterogeneity analysis shows DT’s effect is more significant among enterprises in ETS pilot regions and those with high carbon emissions. This study shifts the focus from innovation quantity to quality in a critical context. Its originality lies in revealing the synergistic effects of digital resources with internal governance (EGA) and strategic orientation (CSR), and providing novel evidence on ETS policy as a boundary condition for unlocking DT’s green potential. We conclude that DT’s effectiveness in driving quality green innovation is contingent on proactive green awareness, social responsibility, and supportive carbon pricing. These findings provide contextual insights into how policy-driven digital transformation interacts with environmental governance to enhance green innovation, offering actionable references for emerging economies undergoing similar low-carbon transitions.

title: The nexus of digital transformation, ESG, and innovation: a bibliometric and systematic review
summary: This study systematically reviews and synthesizes the interaction ecosystem (nexus) among Digital Transformation (DT), Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance, and green innovation through a mixed-method design. By integrating macro-level bibliometric analysis and a micro-level Systematic Literature Review (SLR) adhering to PRISMA guidelines, we address linear and fragmented perspectives in existing literature. We propose a multidimensional conceptual framework integrating the Resource-Based View (RBV), Dynamic Capabilities Theory (DCT), and Institutional Theory. Specifically, we conceptualize a tentative “dual-engine synergy” mechanism defined as the collaborative interaction where digital technologies act as foundational enablers that amplify ESG performance through green innovation as a core mediator with environmental uncertainty functioning as a key moderating boundary condition. Additionally, the review incorporates a critical perspective on the “digitalization paradox” the phenomenon where rapid digital expansion inadvertently increases environmental footprints or induces symbolic compliance. This synthesis aims to strengthen the conceptual foundation of digital sustainability. Finally, we tentatively discuss the potential of Blockchain technology to address ESG rating divergence and suggest Machine Learning as a speculative tool for future empirical validation, highlighting these as hypothetical pathways requiring rigorous empirical testing.

title: Building Business Resilience of Food MSMEs in Tourism Destinations: The Roles of Adaptive Marketing Capability, Supply Chain Resilience, and Digital Transformation Amid Climate and Tourism Disruptions
summary: Food micro, small, and medium enterprises (SMEs) in Bali's tourism destinations face dual pressures stemming from climate disruption and tourism visit volatility. Both forces simultaneously threaten the operational continuity and business resilience of small-scale food businesses that are heavily dependent on the stability of the tourism ecosystem. This study empirically examines the roles of adaptive marketing capabilities (AMC), supply chain resilience (SCR), and digital transformation capability (DTC) in building the business resilience (BR) of food SMEs, as well as the moderating effect of climate and tourism disruption (CTD) on the SCR–BR relationship.A quantitative approach with a cross-sectional survey design was employed, collecting data from 220 food SME owners and managers across Badung Regency, Denpasar City, and Gianyar Regency, Bali. The structured questionnaire instrument used a 5-point Likert scale covering 26 indicators across five latent constructs. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) via SmartPLS 4.0 software, with a 5,000-sample bootstrapping procedure applied for significance testing. All seven hypotheses were supported with statistically significant results. AMC positively and significantly influenced SCR (β=0.449; t=7.242; p<0.001) and directly influenced BR (β=0.162; t=2.077; p<0.05). SCR positively influenced DTC (β=0.528; t=9.103; p<0.001) and directly influenced BR (β=0.249; t=3.320; p<0.01). DTC positively influenced BR (β=0.311; t=4.380; p<0.001). The sequential mediation AMC→SCR→DTC→BR was confirmed as significant with an indirect effect of β=0.074 (BC-CI 95% [0.032, 0.127]). CTD was found to strengthen the effect of SCR on BR (β=0.143; t=2.103; p<0.05). The model collectively explained 46.7% of the variance in business resilience (R²=0.467), with positive Q² values confirming adequate predictive relevance. Adaptive marketing capabilities, supply chain resilience, and digital transformation capability constitute three mutually reinforcing strategic pillars for building business resilience among food SMEs in tourism destinations. The identified sequential mediation mechanism confirms that investment in market adaptive ability progressively translates into supply chain robustness and ultimately catalyzes digital transformation as the foundation of long-term business resilience. As climate and tourism disruption intensifies, enhancing supply chain resilience becomes increasingly critical and of high strategic value. This study contributes theoretically to the dynamic capabilities framework and SME resilience literature, while offering practical recommendations for business practitioners and policymakers in Bali's tourism sector.

title: THE ROLE OF GREEN BONDS IN FINANCING SUSTAINABLE INFRASTRUCTURE: OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES FOR EMERGING MARKETS
summary: Sustainable infrastructure development represents an essential foundation for long-term economic stability and climate resilience across global financial systems. The transition toward low-carbon infrastructure requires sub-stantial long-term capital allocation that public budgets alone cannot sustain. Green bonds have emerged as a piv-otal financial innovation designed to bridge the structural climate financing gap in developing nations. These debt securities contractually commit issuers to allocate raised capital exclusively to certified environmental projects. By establishing clear disclosure frameworks, green debt instruments enhance market transparency and align corpo-rate strategies with global sustainability goals. Institutional investors increasingly deploy green bonds to diversify portfolios while fulfilling environmental, social, and governance mandates.

title: Banco general como actor del desarrollo sostenible en panamá: análisis de la integración de los objetivos de desarrollo sostenible y las finanzas sostenibles en sus reportes corporativos (2023-2025)
summary: Sustainability has become a strategic element for financial institutions due to growing demands for transparency, corporate responsibility and contributions to sustainable development. In this context, banks have assumed a relevant role in promoting responsible economic practices and aligning their strategies with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of the United Nations 2030 Agenda. The objective of this study was to analyze Banco General's role as an actor of sustainable development in Panama through the integration of SDGs, sustainable finance and corporate social responsibility in its corporate reports during the period 2023–2025. A qualitative approach based on a case study design and documentary analysis of sustainability reports and institutional documents was employed. The findings reveal a progressive incorporation of international sustainability standards as well as actions related to financial inclusion, education, environmental management, corporate governance and sustainable finance. A significant alignment with several SDGs was identified, particularly those related to quality education, gender equality, decent work and economic growth, climate action and partnerships for the goals. It is concluded that Banco General has consolidated an institutional strategy oriented toward sustainable development, positioning itself as a benchmark within the Panamanian banking sector in sustainability and social value creation.

title: A Review of Financing Green Innovation: Pathways to Sustainable Development
summary: As there is increasing focus on critical environmental issues such as climate change and global warming from governments, there is an urgent need to examine the factors that enable and encourage green initiatives. Green finance which emphasizes environmentally responsible investments and practices has emerged as a vital tool in achieving neutrality and ensuring sustainable development, economic growth as well. This paper reviews the role of financial assistance and it’s inter connection with sustainable development. The adverse externalities associated with environmental degradation draws attention to the need of sustainable innovation in public management. Green finance provides financial support for R&D activities of renewable energy and sustainable products processes. The analysis will highlight the key issues faced by policymakers and stakeholders to develop and combine two aspects in research and practice to ensure environmental harmony and further promoting long term sustainability. Active collaboration between public and private organisations facilitates the transition of the financial system toward sustainability. Using a hybrid research method that integrates bibliometric analysis and a systematic literature review, the paper identifies major trends, challenges, and opportunities in green finance. Findings highlight that effective financing of green innovation depends on collaborative efforts among governments, financial institutions, and private sectors. The study concludes by proposing strategic pathways to strengthen the financial ecosystem for sustainable development.

title: Corporate audit committees: A focused literature review
summary: Audit committees play an important role in today’s corporate governance systems as they help the board oversee the integrity of financial reporting, the quality of external audits, the effectiveness of internal controls, and, more recently, sustainability and risk reporting. This focused literature review attempts to integrate theoretical and empirical work on corporate audit committees in India and beyond. The review, using seminal works, organizes data on different dimensions of regulatory evolution, applicable theoretical frameworks (agency and resource dependence theories), structural and process characteristics (independence, financial expertise, size, diligence, and diversity), and outcome areas of earnings management, financial reporting, audit, firm performance, fraud and related-party risks, and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) reporting. Against the backdrop of Clause 49, the Companies Act, 2013, and Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements (LODR), Indian data have been interpreted, while global data analyses focus on the post-Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) and international code-based frameworks (Bédard et al., 2004; Chakrabarti et al., 2008). The synthesis confirms the overwhelming consensus on the role of independence and the presence of accounting/financial expertise in driving audit committees’ effectiveness. The paper outlines a multi-level agenda for future studies at the crossroads of regulation, ownership structure, and widening audit committee roles.

title: Semantic fuzzy bat optimization for regional manufacturing supply chain resilience
summary: Regional manufacturing supply chains are experiencing more frequent supplier closures, logistics bottlenecks, severe weather and cascading failures of secondary suppliers. The existing disruption-response systems generally separate textual risk perception from optimisation-based decision-making and are thus unable to convert unstructured warning information into timely recovery plans. This paper introduces a semantic-driven resilience decision engine that combines BERT-based event extraction with a fuzzy-controlled bat algorithm in a perception-decision-execution framework. The Perception Layer converts news reports, enterprise announcements and other operational text into structured disruption vectors that contain information such as event type, intensity, affected entities and estimated duration. The decision layer uses the above semantic signals, as well as population diversity and stagnation status, to adaptively adjust the loudness and pulse rate of the bat algorithm to optimise recovery time, extra cost and service-level maintenance. The execution layer connects the selected strategy with ERP, MES, WMS and transportation interfaces to realise a closed-loop operation. Based on experiments with five manufacturing enterprises, 10,500 labelled disruption records and three representative disruption scenarios were used, and the proposed engine achieved an F1 score of 91.0% for entity extraction and 84.6% for relation extraction. It reduces the number of convergence generations by 37.1% compared to the standard Bat algorithm, is about 37.2% faster than manual decision-making, and has an end-to-end latency of less than four seconds. Based on the above results, a deployable and robust solution for high-frequency supply chain disruption management can be achieved by combining semantic perception with adaptive swarm optimisation.

title: From ethics to metrics: the transformation of corporate social responsibility from good intentions to governance in SME sustainability research
summary: This study examines the development of research on Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), corporate sustainability, and Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) within the context of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). It analyzes 3,168 English-language research articles published from 1959 to 2025, sourced from the Web of Science and Scopus databases, utilizing Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny. Indicators such as annual publication volume, citations, sources, authors, institutions, and countries are evaluated alongside co-citation, country collaboration, co-word, thematic mapping, and thematic evolution analyses. To prevent conflating bibliometric patterns with a paradigm shift, the titles and abstracts of the ten most-cited publications in each period are reviewed for contextual support. The findings demonstrate that 83.7% of publications occur between 2016 and 2025, with no clear peak or deceleration observed within the series. Exploratory curve fitting is therefore regarded as indicative of conditional model behavior rather than a forecast of field maturity. Thematic analysis reveals that CSR language persists, while sustainability, performance, reporting, and ESG terms are added to and reweight the established conceptual core. Resource constraints, owner-manager centrality, informal responsibility practices, and limited reporting capacity characterize the SME context as distinct from that of larger firms. This study provides a reproducible data protocol while maintaining a clear distinction between bibliometric observations and conceptual or practical interpretations.

title: Platform-Enabled AI Adoption and Supply Chain Resilience in Chinese SMEs: an Integrated Theoretical Framework
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is profoundly reshaping the global supply chain landscape. However, the mechanism through which Chinese small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), under resource constraints, acquire AI capabilities through digital platforms and transform them into supply chain resilience has not been adequately theorized. This paper develops an integrated theoretical framework that combines the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework with dynamic capability theory. It proposes the analytical concept of “platform-enabled AI adoption" to characterize the distinctive technology adoption pattern through which Chinese SMEs acquire, integrate, and utilize AI capabilities via external digital platforms. Using a literature review and case analysis approach, and drawing on the 2025 survey report of the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, publicly available operating data from the 1688 platform and Haizhi Online, and relevant academic literature from the past decade, this paper systematically analyzes three mediating pathways through which platform-enabled AI adoption affects supply chain resilience: supply chain visibility, supply chain agility, and supply chain collaboration. It further discusses the moderating roles of technological readiness and organizational readiness in this relationship and offers methodological suggestions for future empirical research. This paper provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the relationship between AI adoption and supply chain resilience among Chinese SMEs in the digital platform context and offers testable research propositions for subsequent empirical examination.

title: ESG Governance and Sustainable Islamic Finance in Malaysia, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia and UAE
summary: Growing dissatisfaction with symbolic ESG compliance has exposed a governance gap in sustainable finance: ethical commitments are expanding faster than mechanisms capable of converting them into measurable environmental and social outcomes. This study examines how ESG governance can function as an institutional bridge between sustainable finance and Islamic finance, with relevance to Malaysia, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Following PRISMA 2020, 29 records identified through Web of Science, Scopus and Emerald Insight were screened, yielding 15 peer-reviewed studies published between 2024 and 2026 for qualitative thematic analysis. Five interconnected themes emerged: normative convergence between ESG and Islamic ethical finance; governance and institutional accountability; Islamic social finance and inclusive sustainability; disclosure, transparency and legitimacy; and digital transformation and impact measurement. The findings show that ethical compatibility alone does not generate credible sustainability outcomes. Strong internal governance, including sustainability committees, Shariah supervisory boards, ESG oversight and integrated reporting, emerges as the critical mechanism separating substantive sustainability from symbolic compliance. Islamic social finance remains notably under-integrated into formal ESG architectures, while existing disclosures are frequently governance-heavy but metric-light. Digital technologies can strengthen traceability and impact measurement, but only when embedded within robust governance systems. This study develops an integrated ESG–Islamic governance framework that translates Maqasid al-Shariah principles into measurable accountability, impact verification and scalable green-development mechanisms. It reframes ESG from a reporting regime into governance infrastructure for ethical, inclusive and resilient finance, offering actionable implications for regulators, financial institutions and sustainability standard-setters.

title: From Counterfeit Detection to Supply Chain Resilience: How Converged Digital Trust Technologies Secure Third-Party Logistics Supply Chains
summary: Counterfeit goods create economic, security, and sustainability risks for supply chains, yet blockchain, radio-frequency identification (RFID), and artificial intelligence (AI) have mostly been studied as separate technologies. This study conceptualises their joint adoption as Logistics Anti-Counterfeiting Digital Technology (LACD) adoption, a converged capability combining identification, traceability, and analytical detection. Drawing on Rational Choice Theory and Deterrence Theory within a perspective informed by the Technology-Organisation-Environment framework, it examines the antecedents and outcomes of LACD adoption and the moderating role of government regulation. Survey data from 232 medium and large third-party logistics (3PL) firms in China were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling. Perceived benefit, deterrent severity, and deterrent certainty were positively associated with LACD adoption, whereas perceived complexity and cost were negatively associated with it; sanction celerity was not significantly associated with adoption. LACD adoption was positively associated with logistics security effectiveness and supply chain resilience. Government regulation strengthened the effects of perceived benefit, deterrent severity, and deterrent certainty and weakened the negative effect of perceived cost, but did not moderate the effects of perceived complexity or sanction celerity. The study also proposes, as an untested proposition, that LACD may provide traceability infrastructure for circular supply chain practices.

title: Redefining Audit Efficiency: A Model for Streamlined Financial Reporting in Nigerian Chartered Accounting Practices
summary: This critical review examines how Nigerian chartered accounting practices can redefine audit efficiency and streamline financial reporting. It applies a structured thematic synthesis of 250 DOI-verified, peer-reviewed and institutional sources published through 2022, coding the evidence across four dimensions: conceptual definition, causal mechanism, empirical support, and implementation constraint. Grounded in agency theory, audit-quality theory, institutional (isomorphism) theory, and lean process-efficiency theory, the synthesis shows that efficiency in Nigerian audit practice follows from standardized workflows, risk-focused procedures, independent audit-committee oversight, staff capability, and timely review, while professional judgment continues to protect audit quality where formal controls are weak. Unlike prior single-determinant studies of Nigerian audit quality, which typically isolate one governance variable at a time, this review's contribution is an integrative operating model that connects audit inputs, workflow design, review discipline, reporting accuracy, and engagement performance into a single framework, together with four testable propositions and a Nigeria-specific research agenda for stronger validation, transparency, and institutional comparison. The review also proposes a repositioned role for chartered accounting firms as active drivers, rather than passive recipients, of digital transformation, continuous auditing, and regulatory reform in Nigeria's financial reporting ecosystem.

title: Legal Challenges In International Commercial Payments With Special Reference To Letters Of Credit In The Digital Economy
summary: International commercial payments make the world go round, and Letters of Credit (LCs) are at the heart of it all, trusted by buyers and sellers everywhere. They’ve been the gold standard for minimizing risk in global trade, mostly thanks to the rules laid out in UCP 600. But times are changing fast. As trade moves online, we’re seeing everything shift: electronic documents, blockchain, fintech apps, digital banks. These new tools are great, but they’re also bringing a whole bunch of legal headaches, think questions about how to validate electronic documents, worries about authentication, cybersecurity, privacy, fraud, cross-border disputes, and keeping up with a patchwork of regulations. This study dives into the legal maze surrounding Letters of Credit in today’s digital economy, focusing on how international payments work now. It takes a hard look at big legal frameworks like UCP 600 and the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Transferable Records (MLETR), plus Indian laws such as the Information Technology Act, FEMA, and various banking rules. The research spots some pretty serious gaps, showing that the current laws aren’t quite keeping pace with new digital risks. In the end, it calls for smarter regulations and fresh policies, so we can better control digital LCs, resolve legal uncertainties across borders, and make international trade safer, faster, and more reliable. All that, with the goal of protecting the integrity of global payments, even as technology keeps changing the game.

title: CSR corporate social responsibility and corporate tax avoidance: the governance role of CSR committees
summary: Purpose This study examines the moderating role of corporate social responsibility (CSR) committees in the relationship between CSR practices and corporate tax avoidance. While CSR is often viewed as an ethical commitment, prior research suggests it may also be used symbolically to legitimize aggressive tax strategies (“tax greenwashing”). This study investigates whether CSR committees act as a substantive governance mechanism that constrains such opportunistic behavior in US NASDAQ-listed firms. Design/methodology/approach Using a panel of non-financial NASDAQ-listed firms from 2012 to 2023, the study employs a generalized least squares (GLS) estimator. This approach is specifically chosen to address heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation within the panel data, while accounting for unobserved firm-level heterogeneity, thereby ensuring the efficiency and statistical reliability of the empirical findings. Findings The results demonstrate that CSR committees significantly moderate the CSR–tax avoidance relationship. While CSR engagement alone shows an ambiguous association with tax behavior, the presence of a dedicated CSR committee is associated with lower levels of tax avoidance. This indicates that specialized governance oversight is essential to prevent the strategic decoupling of social responsibility from fiscal practice. Practical implications The findings highlight the importance of CSR committees for boards, investors, and policymakers as internal governance watchdogs that enhance fiscal accountability and mitigate reputational and regulatory risks related to tax aggressiveness. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by identifying CSR committees as a key boundary condition shaping the ethical integrity of CSR strategies. Evidence from the US context suggests that internal governance structures, rather than CSR disclosure alone, are central to constraining the instrumental use of CSR for tax-related opportunism.

title: Research on the Current Status and Influencing Factors of the Digital Transformation of Small and Micro Enterprises in Shanghai
summary: Enterprise digitalization has become a key measure for enhancing corporate competitiveness and promoting the development of the digital economy. Drawing on questionnaire survey data, this paper quantitatively evaluates the degree of digital transformation of small and micro enterprises in Shanghai along multiple dimensions, including industry, development stage, and position in the industrial chain. On this basis, it constructs an evaluation index system and applies the fuzzy analytic hierarchy process to identify the influencing factors. The results show that, at the criterion level, the participant factor has the greatest impact on the digital transformation of small and micro enterprises in Shanghai, followed in descending order by organizational, task, and technological factors; at the indicator level, the factors with the greatest impact are customer satisfaction, strategic planning for digital transformation, market incentives, and information security and risk prevention and control. Accordingly, this paper puts forward policy recommendations on improving customer satisfaction, refining the market incentive mechanism, attaching greater importance to information security and risk prevention and control, and establishing a multi-dimensional collaborative support system, with a view to advancing the digital transformation of small and micro enterprises in Shanghai.

title: GREEN TRANSFORMATION OF GLOBAL BUSINESS IN THE CONTEXT OF DECARBONIZATION, COMPETITIVENESS, AND INCLUSIVE SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT
summary: The article examines the green transformation of global business in the context of accelerating decarbonization, technological change, and the transition towards sustainable development. The purpose of the study is to substantiate the relationship between decarbonization, business competitiveness, and inclusiveness, as well as to identify the key changes in the sources of competitive advantage caused by the global low-carbon transition. The study analyzes current trends in renewable energy development, clean energy investment, carbon pricing, carbon border regulation, low-carbon technologies, and critical mineral markets. Particular attention is paid to the impact of these processes on corporate strategies, investment decisions, production costs, market access, and the transformation of global value chains. It is established that the green transition is gradually changing the traditional determinants of business competitiveness. Along with productivity, production scale, resource costs, and technological capabilities, carbon and energy efficiency, access to clean energy and green finance, low-carbon innovation, circular business models, supply chain transparency, and compliance with environmental requirements are becoming increasingly important. At the same time, the study demonstrates that the green transformation is characterized by significant geographical, technological, and investment asymmetries. The concentration of renewable energy capacity, green investment, critical mineral processing, and technological capabilities in a limited number of countries and companies creates unequal opportunities for participation in the low-carbon transition and may deepen existing structural disparities in the global economy. The scientific contribution of the study lies in substantiating an integrated approach to the green transformation of global business based on the interrelationship between decarbonization, competitiveness, and inclusiveness. The concept of “inclusive green competitiveness” is proposed to describe the ability of businesses and economic systems to generate sustainable competitive advantages through decarbonization, resource efficiency, green innovation, and technological modernization while simultaneously expanding access to the economic, investment, and technological opportunities created by the green transition and preventing the excessive concentration of its costs and risks among less competitive actors, countries, and social groups. It is concluded that inclusiveness should be considered not only as a social outcome of the green transition but also as an important condition for its long-term economic sustainability. The results of the study can be used to improve corporate strategies and policy approaches aimed at combining decarbonization with competitiveness and inclusive sustainable development.

title: The Effect of Corporate Social Responsibility on Corporate Financial Performance: The Evidence from Borsa Istanbul
summary: Today, the practices implemented by companies within the scope of environmental sustainability have become the focus of attention of investors and researchers within the scope of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR). This study was conducted to determine the impact of CSR on Corporate Financial Performance (CFP). For this purpose, data from companies traded on the Borsa Istanbul (Istanbul Stock Exchange) that have disclosed ESG scores between 2010 and 2020 were used. In the study, market-based financial measure (TOBIN’S Q) and accounting-based measure (ROA) were used as dependent variables. While the ESG score was used as the CSR indicator in the study, sales growth rate, property, plant, and equipment ratio, financial leverage, and dividend paid ratios were also considered control variables. The study findings indicate that CSR practices negatively impact market-based performance and have no significant impact on accounting-based performance. Using Turkey as an example, a developing country, the study emphasizes the importance of companies raising public awareness of their CSR efforts and policymakers supporting market participants through legal regulations. These results offer implications for individuals, investors, business management, societies, and policy practitioners and outline directions for future research.

title: BUSINESS FAILURE AND ACCOUNTABILITY CHALLENGES IN THE NIGERIAN CAPITAL MARKET: CAUSES, CONSEQUENCES AND THE WAY FORWARD
summary: Abstract Business failure remains an important challenge to the development, stability and credibility of the Nigerian capital market. Although corporate failure may arise from legitimate commercial difficulties, persistent weaknesses in corporate governance, financial reporting, internal control, risk management, ethical conduct and regulatory compliance can increase the likelihood that corporate distress will become severe and difficult to reverse. The consequences extend beyond individual companies because shareholders may lose investments, employees may lose employment, creditors may experience losses, government revenue may decline and confidence in the capital market may deteriorate. This paper examines the relationship between business failure and accountability challenges in the Nigerian capital market. It adopts a conceptual review approach based on relevant corporate governance principles, regulatory documents, scholarly literature and institutional publications. The paper identifies weak corporate governance, ineffective boards, inadequate disclosure, financial reporting manipulation, poor internal controls, managerial opportunism, conflicts of interest, weak risk management, audit failures, regulatory compliance problems and ineffective enforcement as major accountability challenges. The paper argues that the existence of corporate governance regulations alone is insufficient unless directors, managers, auditors, regulators and other market participants are held responsible for compliance and misconduct. The Nigerian Securities and Exchange Commission has strengthened its governance framework, including requirements concerning board independence, disclosure and director tenure, while recent regulatory measures also seek to improve the resilience of regulated entities. However, gaps between regulatory requirements and actual implementation remain a concern. The paper recommends stronger enforcement, technology-driven regulatory surveillance, improved board independence, effective audit committees, enhanced financial disclosure, protection of whistle-blowers, greater accountability of directors and auditors, investor education and early-warning mechanisms for financially distressed companies. It concludes that sustainable development of Nigeria's capital market depends not merely on increasing market size and transactions but on building a culture of transparency, responsibility, ethical leadership and enforceable accountability.

title: Interactive effect of ESG performance on the earnings management, tax avoidance and financial performance relation: A bibliometric and empirical analysis
summary: This paper provides a bibliometric and analytical assessment of the salient works examining earnings management, tax avoidance, financial performance, and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) adoption. The research is based on data obtained from the Scopus database between 2016–2026; VOSviewer was used to analyze trends in research, as well as co-occurrence of keywords, citation patterns, and collaborations among countries. The results indicate that previous research is quite focused on the study of earnings management related to financial performance, where few studies link tax avoidance with ESG performance (Friede et al., 2015; Kolsi et al., 2023). The results also suggest that while ESG performance has received increased attention in recent years as a predictor of financial performance/future cash flows or opportunistic behavior, its link to traditional accounting research streams appears weak. Although a substantial body of research has examined earnings management, tax avoidance, financial, and ESG performance, their integrated relationships remain underexplored. This study addresses this gap by developing a unified framework that examines ESG performance as a moderator of the relationships among the other three variables. The conclusions of this study can provide theoretical and practical support for academic circles, enterprises, investors, regulators, and other relevant stakeholders.

title: INVESTIGATING ETHICAL CONSUMERISM IN UZBEKISTAN: THE THEORY OF PLANNED BEHAVIOR
summary: When the market offers enough options, consumers tend to purchase not only based on their needs but also on their conscience. Consumers start to seek clear awareness of manufacturers' or service providers' environmental and social impact when social inclusiveness surfaces in personal behaviors. This study explores the factors influencing ethical consumerism in Uzbekistan using the Theory of Planned Behavior. It is identified that when environmental and social responsibility pressures the purchasing process, consumers act ethically towards attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control. The result of quantitative analysis supports that Uzbek consumers prefer buying from providers who are socially and ecologically supportive. These findings would be supportive information for developing companies' strategic positions, including Corporate Social Responsibility and Environmental, Social and Governance.

title: Geographic proximity of investors and firms' ESG performance: Evidence on local retail and institutional investors
summary: Using EDGAR Log File data to measure active investor information acquisition and MSCI KLD ratings to assess ESG performance, we find that a higher proportion of local investors is positively associated with firms' future ESG performance. Separating local investors into retail and institutional subgroups, we find that both positively influence ESG outcomes and have economically comparable effects, suggesting that local retail investors play at least as important a role as local institutional investors. Three cross-sectional tests reveal that the influence of local retail investors strengthens as information asymmetry falls, managerial entrenchment declines, and the shareholder base widens, while the influence of local institutional investors generally moves in the opposite direction. Two identification strategies, including a headquarters-relocation instrumental variable and a geographic-segment subsample analysis, support causal interpretation. Additional tests show that local retail investors improve workforce diversity but are negatively associated with formal governance ratings, consistent with their reliance on informal local monitoring rather than formal shareholder engagement.

title: Beyond Disclosure: Sustainable Finance Regulation and the Pricing of ESG Performance in Mature Capital Markets
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines whether and under what conditions Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance becomes financially meaningful in mature capital markets. Using a longitudinal transatlantic panel of large firms listed in the EURO STOXX 50 and S&P 100 over the period 2015–2024, we analyse the within‐firm association between lagged ESG performance, market valuation, and accounting profitability. We further examine whether this relationship changes around the 2018 EU Action Plan on Financing Sustainable Growth and the 2021 implementation of the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation, and whether ESG controversies moderate the financial relevance of ESG performance. Firm and year fixed‐effect models show that improvements in ESG performance are positively but only weakly associated with Tobin's Q , whereas no systematic relationship emerges with accounting profitability. Policy interaction models and a dynamic event study provide no evidence of a discrete strengthening of the ESG–valuation relationship for EU‐domiciled firms relative to US‐domiciled firms following the selected regulatory milestones. ESG controversies are directionally associated with weaker ESG value relevance, although the evidence is more pronounced for profitability than for market valuation. Moreover, the Environmental, Social, and Governance pillars are not statistically distinguishable from one another. Among large and highly visible firms, sustainable finance regulation may operate as institutional codification and credibility infrastructure rather than as an abrupt valuation shock, although the evidence is equally consistent with limited statistical power and with measurement error in a domicile‐based indicator of regulatory exposure. The results highlight the conditional and statistically fragile nature of ESG value relevance and should be generalized cautiously beyond institutionally mature capital markets.

title: Supply chain resilience research and the automotive industry: review protocol
summary: This project holds the review protocol for a two-part study of supply chain resilience (SCRES) research: a bibliometric analysis of the Scopus-indexed SCRES literature published between 2008 and 2025, and a PRISMA 2020-guided systematic review of the automotive sub-corpus, coded for how studies define, conceptualise and measure resilience, with particular attention to emerging-market contexts and to Morocco. The protocol specifies the search strategy and record counts, the eligibility criteria, a two-stage independent screening procedure, the closed codebook used for data extraction, the inter-rater reliability design and its decision rule, and the planned sensitivity analysis comparing full-text-coded studies with the whole sample. It was written before screening and coding under this protocol began. The bibliometric search was completed before this deposit, so the protocol is deposited rather than prospectively registered, and the resulting manuscript reports it as such.

title: Corporate social responsibility in South‐East Europe: A cross‐national review
summary: Abstract Scholars have called for the corporate social responsibility (CSR) discourse to be advanced by exploring CSR in different countries. Accordingly, this review presents cross‐national differences in CSR among four South‐East European (SEE) countries—Kosovo, Albania, Croatia and Greece. It addresses the state of the academic literature on CSR in SEE and probes what this literature reveals about the understanding and implementation of CSR in the region. An analysis of 45 CSR‐focused articles across these four SEE countries was undertaken using critical interpretive synthesis (CIS). The academic literature indicates that CSR research in SEE is at an embryonic stage. Similarly, CSR awareness in the region is lower than in other European countries. All four SEE countries demonstrate slow CSR adoption, but differences in implementation arise from their unique national contexts and levels of regional institutionalisation. This review emphasises the importance of a country's level of development for the application of CSR and highlights differences between developed (Greece and Croatia) and developing (Kosovo and Albania) countries. It proposes a typology of CSR practices across four actor levels—(1) company, (2) national, (3) regional and (4) international—and presents a conceptual framework illustrating institutional pressures at each level. Finally, it offers directions for future research to scholars interested in the region and provides guidance for SEE companies seeking to embrace CSR.

title: Digital Capacity of Labour Markets: Regional Assessment
summary: Abstract: This study examines the digital capacity of labour markets amid the global digital transformation and increasing economic volatility. The aim of the article is to assess the digital capacity of labour markets as one of sustainability criteria across the world's macro-regions and to identify the structural, institutional, and human capital factors that shape regional disparities of the world. Digital capacity is conceptualized as a multidimensional construct reflecting economies' ability to generate digital jobs, develop digital skills, integrate advanced technologies, and adapt to structural change. Digital labour market capacity depends upon the ability of an economy to generate digital jobs, provide digital skills, integrate into the digital economy and adapt to technological change. The methodology is designed to assess the ability of labour markets to adapt in the context of the digital transformation of the economy, as well as to determine their potential for the implementation of innovative technologies and the development of digital skills. The study proposes a methodological framework based on the Digital Labour Capacity Index (DLCI), which combines two components: Digital Workforce & Adoption Capacity and Innovation, Research & Advanced Technologies Capacity. The methodology defines a list of key indicators, their reference (base) level values, as well as an algorithm for calculating the Digital Labour Capacity Index (DLCI). A comparative regional assessment covering eight macro-regions reveals substantial disparities in both components and the composite index. East Asia & Pacific demonstrates high levels of DLCI (93.3%), with strong performance across both components reflecting a mature digital ecosystem with rapid technological adaptability. North America (80.0%) and Europe (73.3%) show sufficient levels, formed by well-developed digital skills and innovation infrastructure, though with some internal imbalances. Latin America and the Caribbean records a medium level (46.6%), with digital progress but weak coherence between human capital and technological usage. South Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, and Central Asia and the South Caucasus each register moderate levels (25.0%), constrained by limited digital competencies, low R&D investment, and weak integration into global innovation networks. The Middle East & North Africa shows have low level (13.3%), reflecting simultaneously weak workforce and innovation capacity and a fragmented pattern of digital transformation shaped by raw-material-oriented economic structures. The results suggest that labour market digital capacity is a crucial prerequisite for the sustainable development of global regions. Application of the study methodology reveals pronounced interregional disparities in digital capacity levels. Regions with strong institutional foundations and sustained technology investment – East Asia & Pacific, North America, and Europe – hold clear leading positions, whereas other regions show considerably weaker capacity for digital transformation of their labour markets. These disparities point to the need for differentiated policy responses made to regional specifics, with priority given to human capital development, broader access to digital technologies, and stronger support for innovation activity. The proposed methodology thus offers a practical analytical tool for tracking digital capacity across labour markets, detecting structural imbalances, and informing policy decisions that support sustainable socio-economic development amid ongoing digitalization. Keywords: digital capacity, digital skills, sustainable development, innovation capacity, labour market.

title: Digital Transformation: Are Traditional Auditors' Competencies Sufficient for Remote ISO 14001 Audits?
summary: ABSTRACT This article explores how practitioners perceive the effects of digital transformation on ISO 14001 audits and on the competencies required to conduct them remotely. The study draws on 35 semi‐structured interviews with representatives of ISO‐14001‐certified organizations, external auditors, and consultants. While few studies have examined the digital transformation of ISO 14001 audit practices, this study shows how remote audits reshape verification practices, with greater reliance on documentary evidence and reduced opportunities for direct observation, while increasing the importance of auditors' technological, interpersonal, analytical, and investigative competencies. The analysis of these changes in verification practices and competency requirements contributes to the literature on the perceived rigor of audit evaluations and the credibility of ISO 14001 certification processes. The article contributes to research on the digitalization of assessment tools by showing how digital technologies transform the interpretation mechanisms used by auditors. The results call for adapting auditor training to preserve audit rigor.

title: Green Accounting, Eco-Innovation, and ESG Performance: Dynamic Effects, Mediation, and Threshold Evidence
summary: This study examines the dynamic and non-linear relationships among green accounting (GA), eco-innovation (EI), and ESG performance. Drawing on Legitimacy Theory and the Natural Resource-Based View, the study investigates whether GA and EI independently contribute to ESG performance, whether EI mediates the GA–ESG relationship, and whether a critical level of EI changes the contribution of GA to ESG performance. The analysis uses an unbalanced panel of 500 multinational corporations observed between 2015 and 2025. Two-Step System Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) is employed to address dynamic persistence and potential endogeneity, while Panel Threshold Analysis is used to identify regime-dependent effects. The findings indicate that both GA and EI are positively associated with ESG performance, with EI also functioning as an important transmission mechanism between GA and ESG. Furthermore, the positive contribution of GA becomes substantially stronger when firms exceed a critical eco-innovation threshold of approximately ten green patents per year. ESG performance also demonstrates significant intertemporal persistence. These findings highlight the importance of integrating environmental accounting with substantive innovation capabilities rather than treating sustainability disclosure as an isolated practice. The study offers theoretical implications for sustainability and resource-based perspectives and practical implications for corporate strategy and green policy design.

title: Explaining sustainable performance through digital transformation and green organizational culture: a hybrid PLS-SEM-ANN analysis
summary: This study examines how digital transformation and green organizational culture contribute to sustainable performance through the mediating roles of green innovation and brand equity. Drawing on the resource-based view and dynamic capabilities perspective, the study conceptualizes digital transformation and green organizational culture as strategic resource bases and green innovation and brand equity as distinct resource-conversion mechanisms. Data from 318 managers in Vietnamese manufacturing firms were analyzed using a hybrid PLS-SEM–ANN approach. The PLS-SEM results show that green innovation mediates the effects of both digital transformation and green organizational culture on sustainable performance, whereas brand equity mediates only the effect of green organizational culture. The ANN results further indicate that green organizational culture has greater predictive importance than digital transformation for both green innovation and brand equity. For sustainable performance, PLS-SEM identifies green innovation as the strongest direct predictor, while ANN assigns slightly greater predictive importance to brand equity. These findings highlight asymmetric resource-conversion pathways and demonstrate the complementary value of structural and predictive approaches in explaining sustainable performance. This study contributes to the sustainability and strategic management literature by revealing distinct resource-conversion pathways through which technological and cultural resources shape sustainable performance, while offering practical implications for integrating digital transformation, green organizational culture, and innovation strategies.

title: The Impact of China’s Digital Industrial Cluster Policy on Urban Carbon Quota Development
summary: The digital industrial cluster policy is a key policy instrument for fostering the digital economy and facilitating urban low-carbon transition. Given that no official carbon quota allocation system has yet been established at the city level in China, this paper constructs a multidimensional urban carbon quota index that integrates social, economic, and ecological dimensions, and uses it to measure the carbon quota level of 297 prefecture-level-and-above cities in China over the period 2006–2024. Treating China’s digital industrial cluster policy as a quasi-natural experiment, we employ a staggered difference-in-differences (DID) design to systematically evaluate the policy’s effect on urban carbon quota and the underlying mechanisms. The results show that ① the digital industrial cluster policy significantly raises the urban carbon quota level; ② mechanism tests indicate that this effect is channeled through three paths—stimulating green technological innovation, promoting industrial structure advancement, and improving electricity energy efficiency; ③ heterogeneity analysis reveals that the effect is more pronounced in western regions, in central cities, and in areas with more advanced digital infrastructure and higher carbon quota endowment; ④ spatial econometric results further show that the policy not only enhances local carbon quota but also generates a significant positive spatial spillover effect, raising the carbon quota level of neighboring cities. These findings offer insights for optimizing urban carbon quota allocation through spatial coordination, path coupling, and targeted policy design.

title: Bridging criticality assessment and supply chain resilience : a structured framework for operationalizing mitigation actions
summary: Critical raw materials underpin the energy transition, defense, and digitalization, yet criticality assessments remain diagnostic: they quantify supply risk and vulnerability without prescribing how to act. This gap is addressed through a structured review, from which 139 mitigation actions across mechanisms, capability types, and disruption pathway categories were compiled, harmonized, and classified. A dependency matrix encodes 278 relationships between actions. To operationalize the resulting catalog, a five-stage decision funnel is introduced to filter it by actor-specific structural boundaries and operational readiness. The illustrative application to vehicle electronics shows that no single action is universally applicable, and the set of suitable actions varies with the actor, temporal horizon, degree of control, and disruption profile. By making actor-specific feasibility and inter-action dependencies explicit, the framework enables companies and countries to assemble coherent mitigation portfolios rather than deploying isolated actions whose prerequisites, amplifications, or contradictions remain unexamined.

title: Unravelling the research trend and mapping the intellectual structure of shareholder activism research: a bibliometric analysis
summary: Purpose This paper aims to investigate the knowledge development and the diffusion of shareholder activism (SA) research through a conceptual structure approach. Design/methodology/approach The study builds upon articles indexed in the Scopus database. A systematic search of the articles was done using the keyword search string. After applying all exclusion criteria, 979 research papers from highly recognised journals were retrieved for bibliometric analysis. Findings This research identifies annual publication patterns and highlights influential articles using PageRank analysis. Motor themes, basic, transverse, niche and emerging and declining themes are also determined by using a thematic map. Additionally, this study identifies dominant research themes by dividing the entire research period into sections based on thematic evolution. The paper observed four themes that unite the research in this field: corporate social responsibility (CSR) and SA; return and cost of SA; corporate governance and hedge fund activism; and say-on-pay votes. Moreover, future directions are outlined, such as exploring the mechanisms by which CSR influences SA and identifying which types of CSR practices are more effective at deterring activism. Research limitations/implications This study analysed articles from a single database; however, Scopus provides broader coverage. Further research may broaden the study’s scope by drawing on multiple databases. A quantitative review has limitations that qualitative review methods can overcome, and SA research still has room for additional review methods, such as hybrid review and theoretical review. Practical implications The study provides a useful indicator for academics seeking to understand the emergence of SA, its current dynamics and future research directions. Originality/value The past few years have seen a rise in researchers’ interest in SA. In spite of increased research in this area, the present retrospective study still lacks. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study is the first to provide valuable insights into the conceptual and intellectual structure of SA by applying the bibliometric method optimally. It also suggests future prospects for this research field.

title: Exploring how ESG influences firm financial performance through financial mechanisms boundary conditions and ESG aligned Sukuk
summary: The transition towards sustainable finance has fundamentally reshaped corporate value creation, yet the precise mechanisms linking environmental, social, and governance (ESG) initiatives to firm financial performance remain theoretically fragmented and empirically contested. To systematically disentangle this, this study applies a hybrid literature review methodology that combines macroscopic bibliometric mapping with in-depth microscopic qualitative content analysis. Based on a meticulously curated dataset of 624 peer-reviewed articles from the Web of Science Core Collection (2014–2026). Using a concentrated sub-sample of 45 core studies for rigorous thematic extraction, this research reconstructs the field’s intellectual topography. This study demystifies the transmission by revealing a complex chain-mediated paradigm in which capital pricing and access to financing serve as the central economic conduits, whilst uniquely identifying ESG-aligned Sukuk as a structurally distinct, dual-signalling mechanism for green value creation. This study proposes a conceptual framework arguing that the ultimate financial payoffs of ESG are not universally supported but are strictly governed by exogenous institutional boundary conditions, including investor preferences, institutional support, and government guarantees, thereby providing actionable insights for corporate capital optimisation and macroeconomic green policy design.

title: The impact of peer effect on corporate social responsibility: the moderating role of rent-seeking behavior and stakeholder pressure
summary: This study empirically investigates the impact of peer effects on corporate social responsibility (CSR) performance, incorporating the moderating roles of rent-seeking behavior and stakeholder pressure. Utilizing a panel dataset of 2668 Chinese A-share listed companies from 2015 to 2022, we construct regression models with industry and regional peer effects as explanatory variables, CSR as the dependent variable, and rent-seeking along with multi-dimensional stakeholder pressure as moderators. The results demonstrate that peer effects exert a statistically significant positive influence on CSR performance at the 1% level. Stakeholder pressure and rent-seeking behavior are found to positively moderate this relationship. Furthermore, the influence of peer effects is more pronounced in state-owned enterprises, larger firms, and those with higher profitability, compared to their private, smaller, and less profitable counterparts. This research contributes to the literature by unraveling the intrinsic mechanisms and boundary conditions of peer effects on CSR, offering valuable insights for policymakers and corporate managers aiming to enhance CSR engagement within industrial and regional contexts.

title: TURQUALITY-SUPPORTED COMPANIES IN THE PLASTICS-RELATED SECTOR: A CONTENT ANALYSIS OF SUSTAINABILITY AND DIGITALIZATION VISIBILITY IN CORPORATE REPORTS
summary: In this study, it was aimed to examine the transformation awareness and sustainability visibility of Turquality-supported plastics companies in Türkiye. In the study, the most up-to-date sustainability reports of six Turquality-supported plastics companies were evaluated with content analysis using qualitative research methods. In the analysis, the prominent words in the report were determined by word frequency and word cloud analysis. As a result of the analysis, it was determined that environmental sustainability received the highest emphasis among the reports, followed by social and economic dimensions. Furthermore, digitalization-themed words have also been found to have relatively limited visibility. Looking at the company-level results, it can be said that Brisa and Teklas are the companies with the highest corporate visibility, standing out in the overall sustainability outlook and digital transformation indicators, respectively. The findings provide strategic insights for policymakers and firms, emphasizing the necessity of strengthening digital transformation capacity alongside environmental initiatives to fully realize Turquality’s strategic objectives. This study is one of the first to analyze the intersection of Turquality support and twin transformation in the plastics industry, and is thought to provide empirical insights into how national brand programs promote sustainability-oriented digital competitiveness.

title: INTEGRATED MODEL OF ANALYSIS OF THE STATE OF CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY IN THE SYSTEM OF STRATEGIC MANAGEMENT OF HARMONIOUS DEVELOPMENT
summary: The article analyzes scientific works on the essence and state of corporate social responsibility (CSR) in the system of strategic management of harmonious development. The scientific novelty of the study lies in the formation of a comprehensive model of CSR analysis, which integrates the assessment of internal and external factors with the system of assessment directions. It is determined that the main directions of assessing the state of CSR are the market, working and environmental environment, as well as interaction with society. The practical value of the model lies in the possibility of its use by enterprises to improve the efficiency of CSR management and justify strategic decisions in the field of sustainable development. The proposed model allows ensuring the systematicity and consistency of the CSR assessment process and increases the level of objectivity of the analysis.

title: Analysis of Management Strategy, Corporate Social Responsibility and High-Profile Firm Value In Indonesia
summary: Information regarding Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) can encourage investors to make decisions that enhance firm value. Efficient risk management in operational activities further increases firm value while minimizing potential operational failures. High-profile companies show greater interest in disclosing CSR activities due to high external sensitivity and media coverage. This study examines the moderating effects of risk management and media exposure on the impact of CSR on high-profile firm value in Indonesia from 2016 to 2018. Using a quantitative approach, secondary data from 69 observations were analyzed through Moderated Regression Analysis (MRA). The empirical findings indicate that CSR has a significant positive effect on high-profile firm value. However, neither risk management nor media exposure moderates the relationship between CSR and firm value. These findings suggest that investors evaluate CSR implementation as a direct positive signal rather than focusing on risk disclosures or media coverage. Consequently, companies should prioritize genuine CSR practices to enhance corporate value, while regulators need to establish clearer standards for risk management disclosures.

title: Comparative performance and risk of global ESG and conventional funds (2018–2024)
summary: Purpose This research examines whether environmental, social, and governance (ESG) integration comes at a cost financially through an analysis of the performance of global ESG and traditional funds. Design/methodology/approach Using a global dataset of funds (2018–2024), fixed-effects regressions, and risk-adjusted measures such as the Sharpe ratio, Jensen's alpha, and Drawdown, this paper examines performance differences. Findings Returns from ESG funds are similar to those of regular funds after risk adjustment. More specifically, ESG funds perform better in terms of risk management, with lower volatility (12.15 vs. 13.02%) and maximum drawdowns (−18.4% vs. −21.3%). Such an advantage is especially noticeable in equity funds, which demonstrate not only better performance but also lower volatility. Besides, ESG funds also proved more robust amid COVID-19-related risks, recording losses 1 point lower. Practical implications Integration of ESG provides a “haven” in times of market stress without affecting future gains. The results help investors manage risks and help policymakers justify sustainability finance models. Originality/value This study covers both the coronavirus outbreak and the 2022 energy crisis and offers crucial empirical evidence on the downside protection provided by ESG.

title: Compliance in digital innovation: Managing digital transformation at Treasury Bank
summary: Digital transformation has become a strategic priority for banks seeking to improve operational efficiency, strengthen controls, and remain competitive. In highly regulated environments, however, technology projects cannot be evaluated on operational merit alone; they must also satisfy regulatory, security, audit, and governance requirements. This teaching case examines the implementation of an outsourced Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) high-value payment processing system at ‘Treasury Bank’, a large commercial bank, and traces how compliance shaped decision-making across the entire project lifecycle. What began as a seemingly straightforward automation of a manual, email- and paper-based treasury process evolved into a broader organisational transformation involving Compliance, Risk Management, Information Security, System Audit, Legal, and Data Governance functions. The case follows five implementation phases – project assessment, vendor assessment and business approval, system development, testing and validation, and go-live – showing how governance reviews influenced vendor selection, security assessments, audit requirements, and final approvals. Drawing on interviews with business and IT stakeholders directly involved in the project, the case highlights both the benefits of embedding compliance throughout the transformation, including stronger controls, greater transparency, improved auditability, and higher system quality, and the challenges this approach created, such as additional reviews, increased coordination, and extended timelines. It concludes with the strategic dilemma facing senior management: how to maintain robust compliance and governance while keeping digital transformation responsive and timely. The case suits undergraduate and postgraduate courses in Information Systems, IT Governance, Digital Transformation, and related fields.

title: Exploring the role of green innovation and logistics in linking Logistics 4.0 to sustainable performance: why digitalisation alone is not enough?
summary: The logistics sector operates as a complex sociotechnical system in which digital transformation and environmental sustainability interact as interdependent subsystems. Logistics 4.0 technologies are credited with improving operational efficiency, yet how they translate into performance remains underexplored within an integrated systems framework. Drawing on a systems science perspective, this study examines how Logistics 4.0 affects logistics performance directly and indirectly through green logistics and green innovation. Survey data from 338 manufacturing firms were analysed using structural equation modelling and mediation analysis. All seven hypothesised relationships were supported: Logistics 4.0 predicted green logistics (β = 0.735), green innovation (β = 0.631) and performance (β = 0.532), and both mediators predicted performance (β = 0.647 and 0.419). The mediating channels differ in magnitude: green logistics carries a strong indirect effect (k2 = 0.331) and green innovation a moderate one (k2 = 0.203), indicating that the operational and strategic routes to sustainable performance mature on different horizons. The study contributes by modelling these constructs as complementary subsystems rather than isolated variables, and by differentiating empirically the strength of the two mediating channels. For managers and policymakers, the implication is direct: digitalisation delivers its full return only when planned jointly with sustainability capability.

title: Nonlinear Dynamics of Green Innovation, Environmental Regulation, and Corporate Carbon Abatement
summary: Corporate carbon abatement is commonly modeled as a direct and continuous response to environmental regulation or green innovation. Such representations cannot fully explain persistent differences among firms facing similar policy conditions or distinguish the pressure required to initiate a low-carbon transition from that needed to sustain it. This study develops a three-state continuous-time model linking corporate carbon abatement, accumulated green innovation, and effective regulatory pressure, with green market preference treated as an external demand-pull parameter. Green innovation lowers the marginal cost of abatement, abatement generates learning and commercial returns to innovation, and regulatory pressure responds to residual emissions while relaxing as abatement and credible green capability improve. The regulation--innovation channel is non-monotonic: moderate pressure strengthens innovation incentives, whereas the marginal stimulus declines at high pressure. The analysis combines equilibrium and stability analysis, saddle-node verification, attraction-basin classification, temporary-policy simulations, regime mapping, and global sensitivity analysis. Under the baseline configuration, two locally stable equilibria are separated by a saddle, and nondegenerate saddle-node thresholds generate hysteresis between low- and high-abatement states. Green market preference lowers the transition threshold, while temporary regulation succeeds only when both intensity and duration are sufficient. Regulatory adjustment may generate damped oscillatory modes, but no Hopf crossing is detected within the examined range. The findings show that regulatory pressure acts as an adaptive state-transition mechanism through which initial capability, policy timing, and market demand shape persistent corporate carbon-abatement outcomes. Broader stress tests confirm that bistability is conditional and can disappear under weak innovation capacity or combined adverse structural conditions. The numerical procedures developed here---multistart root finding,adaptive Runge--Kutta integration, analytical Jacobian evaluation,and Latin-hypercube sensitivity design---are transferable tocontinuous-time state-transition models in other applied domains.

title: Digital transformation of international organisations: navigating between utopia and shipwreck
summary: Introduction Digital transformation promises greater efficiency and cooperation among international organisations but also risks fragmentation, weakened sovereignty, and exclusion. This paper uses regime complex theory to examine how international organisations navigate these competing pressures. Methods A structured, focused comparative case study approach is applied to selected regional frameworks and international organisation initiatives, including ASEAN’s Digital Economy Framework Agreement, APEC’s Cross-Border Privacy Rules, UNDP’s Digital Strategy, and WFP’s Building Blocks. Documentary analysis examines institutional overlap, authority relationships, and actor strategies. Results The analysis identifies six interconnected governance dimensions: institutional foundations, sovereignty–interoperability tensions, digital public goods, algorithmic diplomacy, cybersecurity, and implementation pathways. Across cases, effective digital transformation depends on legitimacy, accountability, and stakeholder trust. Flexible coordination helps manage sovereignty–interoperability tensions, while AI bias and unequal cybersecurity capacities require inclusive oversight and collective responses. Discussion Digital transformation in international organisations is fundamentally a political rather than merely technical challenge. The paper proposes a minimum-variable governance framework and a four-phase implementation roadmap to balance innovation with institutional integrity. These proposals emphasise adaptive governance, equity, and sustained institution-building as foundations for sustainable digital transformation.

title: How Digital Infrastructure Drives Urban Green Innovation Efficiency: Evidence from Chinese Cities
summary: A balanced panel of 284 Chinese prefecture-level cities covering 2010–2021 is used to examine the relationship between digital infrastructure and urban green innovation efficiency (EUGI). We construct an entropy-weighted index to measure digital infrastructure, while EUGI is estimated through a super-efficiency SBM model that incorporates undesirable outputs. The empirical results indicate that better digital infrastructure is associated with higher EUGI. This positive relationship remains statistically significant after using alternative measures, introducing more restrictive fixed effects, applying instrumental-variable specifications to address endogeneity, and accounting for spatial dependence. Similar evidence is obtained from the Broadband China pilot. The estimates from both the conventional DID model and the Callaway–Sant’Anna approach, which accounts for different policy adoption times, are positive. We also investigate three possible channels underlying this relationship. The estimates are consistent with the roles of green technological innovation, entrepreneurial activity, and industrial upgrading. Formal interaction tests further show that the relationship between digital infrastructure and EUGI differs across regions, between resource-based and non-resource-based cities, and according to the level of local policy support. Overall, the results indicate that digital infrastructure development does not necessarily produce equal green innovation gains across cities. The extent to which digital capacity is translated into green innovation outcomes is also shaped by local innovation resources, industrial conditions, and policy support. Digital infrastructure investment should thus be combined with measures that reflect local innovation and industrial conditions rather than following a uniform policy approach.

title: Governance Framework and Overall Readiness for AI Enabling in Supply Chain Management in Bangladesh
summary: Digital transformation in Supply Chain Management in Bangladesh’s RMG and SME sectors has become very popular because of the need for transparency and digital compliance by foreign customers as well as demand forecasting, inventory control, logistics, traceability and operational decision-making. But most organizations could not implement Artificial Intelligence and digital technology yet. The research reviews several academic papers, industry surveys, institutional reports, government sources and other secondary sources to investigate how prepared Bangladesh is to enable, use and maintain digital technologies like Artificial Intelligence in its supply chain management and what the challenges are there. Studies suggest that high cost of implementation, insufficient number of experts, weak digital infrastructure and the unreadiness of employees and supply chain partners to adapt to a new system are the very obstacles in implementing AI not just in Supply Chain Management but also in various other departments of an organization. Other than that, big firms like export-oriented firms tend to be more prepared than SMEs in accepting advanced digital systems due to a financial and technological edge. To understand this unevenness, this research proposes a ‘Two-axis Digital Readiness Matrix’ which is based on an organization’s internal capability and digital connectivity with external supply-chain partners. This study recommends higher opportunities for financing, advancement of workforce skills, increase in management capability and digital integration among supply chain participants

title: Supply Chain Disruptions and Transparency: The Role of Customer Trust in Building Brand Loyalty
summary: Abstract Purpose – This research explores the disruption in supply chain and transparency level impact on brand loyalty, by a mediating factor of customer trust. It responds to the increasing fragility of supply chains under volatile conditions and examines transparency as a strategic tool to maintain consumer relations. Design/methodology/approach – The cross-sectional survey-based quantitative research design was adopted Simple Random Sampling, a Probability Sampling Technique was used and Data were gathered from 395 consumers who are active digitally through a structured questionnaire and analyzed by Partial PLS-SEM using SmartPLS 3. Findings – Results indicates both supply chain disruption and customer trust are strong predictors of brand loyalty, and transparency has strong positive impacts on these outcomes. Customer trust is observed is an important driver of brand loyalty and mediates the relational between disruption, transparency and loyalty. The mediation analysis showed significant indirect effects customer trust. The model revealed good explanatory power, with R² = 0.755 for brand loyalty and R² = 0.738 for customer trust. Practical implications – Companies need to focus on transparency and building trust through communication and traceability to help mitigate the impact of disruption and maintain consumer loyalty. Originality/value – This research fills a theoretical and empirical void by combining disruption, transparency, and trust in one model, which has practical implications for resilience and competitive advantage in volatile markets.
